extracted.intended_audience: federal agency staff, regulated entities, and members of the public participating in rulemaking and information-collection review
extracted.subtask_description: Explains OIRA's role, review standards, and how agencies and the public should participate in federal rulemaking and Information Collection Request (ICR) review under the Paperwork Reduction Act. Covers significance thresholds, required analyses, disclosure rules, ICR procedures, and public-comment mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation is a general statement issued by an agency, board, or commission that has the force and effect of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress often grants agencies authority or discretion to issue regulations. Federal regulations specify the details and requirements necessary to implement and enforce legislation enacted by Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking process (notice-and-comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal regulations are created through a process known as 'rulemaking,' governed by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Agencies typically publish a proposed rule in the Federal Register, solicit public comments, consider the feedback and make changes where appropriate, then publish a final rule with an effective date and must describe and respond to public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View the Reg Map® for a graphical illustration. The APA generally requires public notice and comment prior to enacting new regulations, and lays out the process for judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) requirement for public notice and comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA generally requires agencies to provide public notice and seek comment prior to enacting new regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA also provides procedures for judicial review of rules; agencies must follow notice-and-comment unless a statutory exception applies (e.g., 'good cause' for bypassing notice in certain interim final rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866 principles (cost–benefit and reasoned determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 12866 requires agencies, for all significant regulatory actions, to analyze costs and benefits and, to the extent permitted by law, act only upon a reasoned determination that the benefits justify the costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EO 12866 aims to enhance planning and coordination, reaffirm agency primacy, restore integrity of regulatory review, and make the process more accessible. Agencies must provide an explanation of the need for regulatory action and an assessment of potential costs and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13563 additional regulatory principles
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 13563 emphasizes protecting public health/safety/environment while promoting economic growth, predictability, use of least burdensome tools, and taking account of quantitative and qualitative benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EO 13563: (1) promote public participation and transparency (e.g., use regulations.gov), (2) reduce redundant/inconsistent/overlapping requirements, (3) identify and consider flexible approaches (warnings, disclosures, etc.), (4) promote scientific integrity, and (5) produce plans for retrospective analysis of existing significant regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'significant' regulatory actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EO 12866 (as amended by EO 14094), OIRA determines which regulatory actions are 'significant.' Significant actions are those that: (a) have an annual effect on the economy of $200 million or more (adjusted every 3 years); or (b) adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector, productivity, competition, jobs, environment, public health or safety, or governments/communities; or (c) create a serious inconsistency or interfere with another agency's action; or (d) materially alter budgetary impacts of entitlements/grants/user fees/loans or rights/obligations; or (e) raise legal or policy issues for which centralized review would meaningfully further the President's priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant regulatory actions must be reviewed by OIRA before publication. OIRA typically designates between 500–700 regulatory actions as significant each year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'economically significant' regulatory actions
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset of OIRA-designated significant actions: 'economically significant' if likely to have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or otherwise materially adverse effects as listed for significant actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For economically significant regulations, EO directs agencies to provide a more detailed assessment of likely benefits and costs, including quantification, and to analyze potentially effective and reasonably feasible alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and standards for regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis is a tool to anticipate and evaluate likely consequences of rules (costs and benefits) and to organize evidence on key effects of alternatives when developing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposes include (1) learning if benefits justify costs, (2) promoting accountability to the public, and (3) identifying alternatives with highest net-benefits. Agencies must assess both quantitative and qualitative benefits and costs and propose/adopt regulations on a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs. OMB publishes 'best practices' guidance (most recently Circular A-4, 2023) to define good regulatory analysis and standardize measurement/reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review purposes and coordination role
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA coordinates interagency Executive Branch review of significant regulations to ensure agency compliance with EO 12866 principles, including incorporation of public comment, consideration of alternatives, and costs/benefits analysis; and to coordinate with other agencies to avoid inconsistent, incompatible, or duplicative policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA review helps ensure agencies carefully consider consequences of rules and that the President's policies/priorities are reflected in agency rules. See Memorandum of Agreement for special cases (e.g., tax regs).

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review timeframe and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The period for OIRA review is limited by EO 12866 to 90 days; there is no minimum. The review may be extended indefinitely by the head of the rulemaking agency; alternatively, the OMB Director may extend review one time for no more than 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and OIRA may therefore have longer review depending on agency request or Director extension; OIRA designates typical volumes of significant reviews annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: When OIRA 'returns' a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: During OIRA's review the Administrator may return a rule to the agency for reconsideration if the rule is not compatible with the law, the agency's analysis is inadequate, the regulation is not justified by the analysis, not consistent with EO 12866 principles or Presidential priorities, or unnecessarily conflicts with other Executive Branch regulations/efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A return letter explains why further consideration would benefit the rulemaking; return does not necessarily imply opposition. See reginfo.gov/eoReturnLetters for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency withdrawal of a rule during review
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may withdraw its rule from OIRA review at any time, choosing not to move forward or to resubmit after further consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interested parties may contact the agency directly about specific withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA disclosure and transparency policies for meetings and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA's policy is to meet with any party interested in discussing issues on a rule under review. Meetings during review must be conducted by the Administrator or a designated official. OIRA keeps a log and makes public substantive communications with any party outside the Executive Branch concerning regulatory actions under review: subject, date, participants, and written materials received are disclosed on the OIRA website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups/individuals can request meetings via the form on Reginfo.gov. After a regulatory action is published in the Federal Register, OIRA will make available certain documents exchanged between OIRA and the rulemaking agency during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of draft documents under review
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft documents under review are considered deliberative and are not available for public release during review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits the public's ability to view draft text until OIRA review concludes; certain materials become public after publication in the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: How outside parties should participate in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to participate is to submit comments directly to the agency during the proposed rule stage (see the Federal Register notices) and/or file comments via regulations.gov. Parties may also provide written comments to the OIRA Administrator on a regulatory action under review and may request meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting comments through regulations.gov is the standard; for ICRs, comments can be submitted to OIRA during the first 30 days of ICR review via Reginfo.gov. Use the EO 12866 Meeting Request page to request OIRA meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Dashboard / Reginfo.gov functions and displayed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Reginfo.gov displays regulatory actions and information collections currently at OIRA for review. The Regulatory Dashboard graphically displays regulatory actions by agency, length of review, economic significance, and stage of rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When individual rule entries are blank it may be because the agency did not provide descriptions in its Unified Agenda entries. Reginfo.gov is distinct from Regulations.gov (which hosts published documents and comment portals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types/stages of regulatory actions displayed
rubrics_metrics.description: Dashboard categories include: Notice; Pre-rule (advance notice of proposed rulemaking); Proposed rule; Final rule; Interim Final Rule (issued under 'good cause' allowing immediate effect with later comment); Direct Final Rule (no post-publication comment period for uncontroversial actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim final rules typically still allow post-publication comment and possible revision. Direct final rules are categorized as final rules for display purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) scope and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRA (1980, reauthorized 1995) provides the statutory framework for federal collection, use, and dissemination of information. Goals include minimizing paperwork/reporting burdens on the public and ensuring maximum utility of collected information. The PRA requires agencies to seek public comment on proposed information collections and to submit proposed collections for OMB review and approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Information' is broadly defined to include statements/estimates of fact or opinion in any form, recordkeeping requirements, third-party disclosures, forms, surveys, etc. The PRA applies when identical questions or reporting/recordkeeping are posed to ten or more 'persons' (individuals, businesses, governments). It applies to voluntary and mandatory collections and those required to obtain federal benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Collection Request (ICR) process and public comment periods
rubrics_metrics.description: ICR process: agency publishes a Federal Register notice providing 60 days for public comment on the proposed collection; agency considers comments and revises as appropriate; agency submits the ICR to OMB and publishes a second Federal Register notice announcing start of OMB review and providing an additional 30 days for comment; OIRA then approves, disapproves, returns, or takes other action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under certain circumstances agencies may request 'emergency' review and approval where normal process would result in public harm or be impossible; emergency requests must explain the reason and take practicable steps to consult with the public. For ICRs related to proposed/final regulations, contents may remain non-public until review is completed and rules are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of ICRs and when public comment is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven ICR types on the ICR Dashboard: New collection; Revision (substantive change); Extension without change; Reinstatement without change; Reinstatement with change; Existing collection in use without OMB Control Number; Discontinue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive or significant revisions generally require public comment (similar to new collections). Non-material or ministerial changes may be treated as technical and not require comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Control Number assignment and display
rubrics_metrics.description: When OMB approves an information collection it assigns an OMB Control Number that the agency must display on the information collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control number is two four-digit codes separated by a hyphen; first identifies sponsoring agency/bureau, second identifies the particular collection. Multiple collections submitted as one ICR may share the same Control Number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions OIRA can take on ICRs
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA can: Approve; Mark as Improperly Submitted; Accept a Withdrawal; or Disapprove an ICR. OIRA may approve for up to three years and may approve with or without change. For ICRs related to proposed rules, OMB may instruct the agency to resubmit at the final stage ('file comment').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If OIRA disapproves an ICR, the PRA states the agency may not proceed with the information collection and that 'no person shall be subject to any penalty for failing to comply' with the collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria OIRA evaluates during ICR review
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA evaluates whether the collection: (1) is necessary for the proper performance of the agency's functions, including whether the information has practical utility; (2) minimizes Federal information-collection burden, especially on those most adversely affected; and (3) maximizes practical utility and public benefit from information collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA also reviews consistency with applicable laws, regulations, and policies related to privacy, confidentiality, security, information quality, and statistical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to participate in the information-collection review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public are encouraged to monitor agencies' Federal Register notices seeking comments on information collections and to provide feedback on those that interest them. The ICR Dashboard provides an easy way to see collections under review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At any point members of the public may also submit comments to sponsoring agencies and OIRA about approved collections (e.g., need for information, reporting burdens). Use the 'Comment' button on Reginfo.gov View ICR pages for ICRs open for public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential Business Information (CBI) and submission restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit information whose disclosure is restricted by statute (trade secrets, commercial/financial information) as Confidential Business Information (CBI) to www.reginfo.gov. Comments submitted through reginfo.gov cannot be claimed as CBI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted via Reginfo.gov will waive any CBI claims for information submitted. If confidentiality is required, contact the sponsoring agency for appropriate submission channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: How OIRA will use and disclose comments and commenter information
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic comments submitted through Reginfo.gov will be maintained in ROCIS and OIRA is the official custodian. The information and materials submitted may be seen by various people; personally identifiable information included in comments may be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted online will not be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov until OIRA concludes review; only verified comments will be publicly disclosed when review is completed. Reginfo.gov offers public data in XML which may include commenter info if included in posted submissions. Contact information provided with comments submitted online will not be publicly disclosed on www.reginfo.gov and may only be used by OIRA; see the site's Privacy Policy for details.
